Facts look like 'intent:advice', 'concept:lease', 'isa:crime' (taxonomy, inherited), 'domain:property_law', 'kw:<word>' (stemmed automatically), 'negation', 'first_person'. In 'all', a nested list is an OR-group. Rules with 'none' (negation-as-failure) run only after all positive rules have finished.

rules.description: Wages are unpaid, late or too low
User has been defamed (any kind of defamation, via inheritance)
User is accused of a crime
A crime is mentioned and the user is NOT the accused -> treat as victim
Any kind of contract (via inheritance) + a breaking verb
User wants to take someone to court
Every civil claim is subject to a limitation period
Every civil claim depends on evidence

then.tip: If you or anyone else is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number first.
Act promptly: most claims must be started within a limitation period, after which you may lose the right to sue.
Keep copies of every document, message, photo and receipt; evidence is what wins disputes.

advice.title: Security deposit not returned
steps: Check your lease for the deposit terms; many places require landlords to return the deposit, or itemise deductions, within a fixed number of days after you move out.
Gather evidence: move-in/move-out photos, the inventory or checklist, rent receipts and messages with your landlord.
Ask for the deposit back in writing, stating the amount and a deadline. Landlords can usually deduct only for unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear.
If the deposit was meant to be held in a deposit-protection or escrow scheme, use that scheme's free dispute service.
If the landlord still refuses, send a formal legal notice or file a claim in small claims court.

advice.title: Facing eviction
steps: Don't ignore any notice. Read it carefully and note the reason given and every deadline.
In most places a landlord must follow a legal process (proper written notice and usually a court order). Changing the locks or removing your belongings without one is generally unlawful.
Check whether the stated reason (e.g. unpaid rent, end of the lease term) is valid under your lease and local tenancy law.
Keep paying rent if you can and keep records of payments; it strengthens your position.
Contact a tenants' rights organisation or legal aid service quickly. You may be able to challenge the eviction or negotiate more time.

advice.title: Rent increase
steps: Check your lease: during a fixed term the rent usually cannot be raised unless the lease allows it.
Landlords normally must give written notice of an increase in advance; check the notice period that applies where you live.
Some areas have rent-control or rent-stabilisation limits. Check with your local housing authority.
If you believe the increase is unlawful or excessive, reply in writing and ask a tenants' association for help.

advice.title: Landlord not making repairs
steps: Report the problem to your landlord in writing, describe it clearly and ask for the repair by a reasonable date.
Take dated photos and keep copies of all communications.
Landlords are generally required to keep the property safe and habitable (water, heating, structure, electrics).
If nothing happens, contact your local housing or building-standards authority. Some places allow rent to be withheld or reduced, but only through the proper legal procedure, so get advice first.

advice.title: Terminated from your job
steps: Ask your employer to give the reason for termination in writing, and collect your employment contract, offer letter, payslips and any warning letters.
Check whether the notice period (or pay in lieu of notice) in your contract and local law was honoured.
Consider whether the dismissal could be linked to discrimination, a complaint you made, pregnancy or taking legal leave. These are commonly unlawful reasons.
Make sure you receive all final pay, unused leave and benefits you are owed.
Raise a written grievance, or approach the labour department or employment tribunal. Strict time limits often apply.

advice.title: Unpaid or underpaid wages
steps: Compare what you were paid with your contract, payslips and the hours you actually worked (including overtime).
Ask your employer in writing for the missing amount and a date for payment.
Paying below the legal minimum wage or withholding earned wages is unlawful in most jurisdictions.
If you are still unpaid, file a complaint with the labour department or wage authority, or bring a claim (small claims court may be an option).

advice.title: Harassment or discrimination at work
steps: Write down every incident: the date, time, what happened, who was involved and any witnesses.
Save emails, chat messages and other evidence somewhere outside work systems.
Report it under your employer's grievance or anti-harassment policy (HR or a manager) and keep a copy of your complaint.
Employers are generally required to investigate and must not retaliate against people who complain.
If your employer fails to act, complain to the relevant equality or labour authority, or consult an employment lawyer.

advice.title: Someone is spreading false statements about you
steps: Preserve evidence: dated screenshots with URLs, recordings, or the names of people who heard it.
Defamation generally needs a false statement of fact (not opinion), communicated to others, that harms your reputation.
For online posts, report the content to the platform.
Consider a cease-and-desist letter or legal notice demanding removal and a retraction.
If you suffered serious harm, a lawyer can advise on claiming damages or an injunction.

advice.title: Personal injury
steps: Get medical attention first, and keep all medical records and bills.
Record evidence: photos of the scene and injuries, witness contacts, and any incident or police report.
Don't admit fault or accept a settlement before you understand what your claim is worth.
A negligence claim usually needs a duty of care, a breach of that duty, and proof the breach caused your injury.
Notify insurers promptly and speak to a personal-injury lawyer; many work on a no-win-no-fee basis.

advice.title: Neighbour dispute (noise or trespass)
steps: Try a calm conversation first; many disputes are simple misunderstandings.
Keep a log of incidents (dates, times, duration) plus any recordings or photos.
If talking fails, send a polite written request, then consider community mediation.
Persistent noise can often be reported to the local council or environmental-health authority.
As a last resort a court can award damages or grant an injunction for nuisance or trespass.

advice.title: Arrested or accused of a crime
steps: Stay calm and do not resist arrest, even if you think it is unjust.
You generally have the right to remain silent. Politely say you want a lawyer before answering questions.
Ask to contact a lawyer (or request a public defender or legal aid lawyer) and to inform a family member.
Don't sign statements you do not understand, and don't discuss the case with other people in custody.
Ask whether bail is available and what conditions apply.

advice.title: Domestic violence
steps: If you are in immediate danger, call your local emergency number now.
Contact a domestic-violence helpline for confidential support and safety planning.
You can usually apply to a court for a protection or restraining order (an injunction).
Keep evidence safely: photos of injuries, medical records, messages and a diary of incidents.
Legal aid is often available in domestic-violence cases.

advice.title: Scam, fraud or hacking
steps: Contact your bank or payment provider immediately to block cards and dispute or reverse transactions.
Change your passwords and turn on two-factor authentication for affected accounts.
Save all evidence: messages, emails, website links and transaction IDs.
Report it to the police or your national cybercrime reporting portal.
Beware of 'recovery' services asking for upfront fees; they are often a second scam.

advice.title: Victim of a crime
steps: If you are in danger, contact emergency services immediately.
Report the crime to the police and get a copy or reference number of the report (police report / FIR).
Preserve evidence: photos, receipts, messages, nearby CCTV locations and witness details.
If property was taken, notify your insurer and, for cards or phones, your bank or mobile carrier.
Victim-support services can help, and you may be entitled to compensation.

advice.title: Faulty product or poor service
steps: Contact the seller first with your receipt or proof of purchase and describe the problem.
Consumer law generally entitles you to a repair, replacement or refund when goods are faulty or not as described, in addition to any manufacturer warranty.
Put your complaint in writing and set a deadline for a response.
If you paid by card, ask your bank about a chargeback.
If the seller refuses, escalate to a consumer protection authority, consumer court or small claims court.

advice.title: Breach of contract
steps: Read the contract carefully to identify the exact obligation that was broken and any dispute-resolution clause.
Collect evidence: the signed contract, invoices, messages and proof that you performed your side.
Send a written demand or legal notice asking the other party to perform or pay compensation within a set time.
Consider mediation or arbitration; many contracts require it before going to court.
If it is still unresolved, you may sue for damages or, in some cases, specific performance.

advice.title: Intellectual property infringement
steps: Document the infringement (screenshots, URLs, dates) and keep proof of when you created your original work.
Identify the right involved: copyright (creative works), trademark (brand names and logos) or patent (inventions).
Check whether an exception such as fair use / fair dealing might apply.
Send a cease-and-desist notice, or file a takedown request with the platform hosting the content.
An IP lawyer can advise on seeking an injunction and damages.

advice.title: Divorce
steps: Find out the grounds and residency requirements for divorce where you live (many places allow no-fault divorce).
Gather financial documents: income, assets, debts, property records and any prenuptial agreement.
Consider mediation to agree on property, support and children; it is usually faster and cheaper than court.
Arrangements for children are decided according to the best interests of the child.
Have a family lawyer review any settlement before you sign it.

advice.title: Child custody and support
steps: Courts decide custody on the best interests of the child: stability, care, and the child's relationship with each parent.
Keep records of your involvement in the child's life (school, medical, day-to-day care).
Try to agree on a parenting plan directly or through mediation.
Child support is usually calculated from official guidelines based on both parents' incomes.
Never withhold access or support to pressure the other parent; it can count against you.

advice.title: Wills and inheritance
steps: To make a valid will you generally need to be an adult of sound mind and sign it in front of witnesses (formalities vary).
Name an executor you trust, keep the will somewhere safe and tell the executor where it is.
Review your will after major life events such as marriage, divorce or having children.
When someone dies, the executor usually applies for probate before distributing the estate.
If there is no will, the estate passes under intestacy (succession) law.

advice.title: Taking legal action
steps: Make sure you have a recognised legal claim and evidence to support it.
Check the limitation period; claims filed too late are usually barred.
Send a legal notice or demand letter first. Many disputes settle at this stage, and courts often expect it.
For low-value disputes, small claims court is simpler and cheaper, and you may not need a lawyer.
Consider mediation or arbitration as faster alternatives to a full trial.

advice.title: You received a legal notice
steps: Don't ignore it; note the deadline for your response.
Read it carefully to understand exactly what is being claimed and demanded.
Gather every document related to the dispute.
Have a lawyer draft or review your reply, because what you write can be used later in court.

advice.title: Finding affordable legal help
steps: Check whether you qualify for legal aid; eligibility usually depends on income and the type of case.
Try law-school legal clinics, bar-association referral services and non-profit legal organisations.
Many lawyers offer a free or low-cost first consultation.
For small disputes, small claims court is designed for people without lawyers.

advice.title: General guidance: tenancy and property
steps: Your lease is the starting point; read the clauses relevant to your issue.
Communicate with your landlord or tenant in writing and keep copies.
Local housing authorities and tenants' associations give free advice.

advice.title: General guidance: employment
steps: Check your employment contract, staff handbook and payslips first.
Raise concerns in writing with HR or your manager and keep copies.
The labour department, a trade union or an employment lawyer can advise on your rights.

advice.title: General guidance: contracts
steps: Read the whole contract, including the small print and any dispute-resolution clause.
A valid contract needs offer, acceptance, consideration and capacity.
Put any change or complaint in writing and keep signed copies.

advice.title: General guidance: civil wrongs (torts)
steps: Write down what happened while it is fresh, and keep evidence of the harm and your losses.
Try to resolve it directly or through mediation first.
A lawyer can tell you whether you have a claim for damages.

advice.title: General guidance: criminal matters
steps: If a crime is happening or someone is in danger, contact the police or emergency services.
If you are questioned or accused, ask for a lawyer before answering.
Legal aid is commonly available in criminal cases.

advice.title: General guidance: family matters
steps: Family disputes are often best settled by agreement or mediation.
Keep financial records and any agreements in writing.
A family lawyer can explain how local law applies to you.

advice.title: General guidance: consumer matters
steps: Keep receipts, order confirmations and warranty documents.
Complain to the seller in writing first.
Consumer protection authorities and consumer courts handle unresolved complaints.

advice.title: General guidance: intellectual property
steps: Keep dated records proving when you created your work or invention.
Trademarks and patents usually need registration; copyright usually arises automatically.
Speak to an IP lawyer before publicly disclosing an invention.

advice.title: General guidance: court process
steps: Check deadlines (limitation periods) before anything else.
Try a demand letter, negotiation or mediation before going to court.
Legal aid and small claims court can make the process affordable.

advice.title: General guidance: wills and estates
steps: Keep your will and estate documents up to date and somewhere safe.
Executors should get legal guidance on probate requirements.
A power of attorney lets someone act for you if you cannot.

rules.description: User wants to report a crime to the police
User wants information from a public authority
User wants to go to a consumer commission
A fundamental right may have been violated

advice.title: Filing an FIR (police complaint)
steps: Go to the police station with jurisdiction over the place where the offence happened. If that is not practical, any police station must register a Zero FIR and transfer it.
Give the information orally or in writing. Oral information must be written down, read back to you and signed by you.
Collect your free copy of the FIR and note its number.
Many states let you file an e-FIR online through the state police website; you must then sign it at the police station within 3 days.
If the police refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence, send your complaint in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police (section 173(4) BNSS).
If that fails, apply to the Magistrate, who can order the police to investigate (section 175(3) BNSS).

advice.title: Filing an RTI application
steps: Write a short application naming the public authority and the exact information you want. You do not have to give reasons.
Address it to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of that office and pay the fee (Rs 10 for central government offices; states set their own). People below the poverty line pay no fee.
For central government offices you can apply online at rtionline.gov.in.
The PIO must reply within 30 days, or within 48 hours if the information concerns someone's life or liberty.
If you get no reply or an unsatisfactory one, file a first appeal with the First Appellate Authority within 30 days.
If it is still unresolved, file a second appeal with the Central or State Information Commission within 90 days.

rules.description: Advice: complaint to a consumer commission

advice.title: Filing a consumer complaint
steps: Write to the seller or service provider first, describing the problem and the remedy you want, and keep proof of what you sent.
You can also contact the National Consumer Helpline (1915), which tries to settle complaints with companies for free.

If that fails, file a complaint with the District Consumer Commission for claims up to Rs 50 lakh (State Commission up to Rs 2 crore; National Commission above that). You can file online through e-Daakhil.
File within 2 years of the problem arising. You can file where you live or work, and you do not need a lawyer.
Attach bills, warranty cards, photos and your correspondence as evidence.

advice.title: Cheque bounce
steps: Keep the returned cheque and the bank's return memo showing why it was not paid.
Send a written demand notice to the person who issued the cheque within 30 days of receiving the return memo.
They then have 15 days from receiving your notice to pay.
If they do not pay, file a complaint before the Magistrate within one month after those 15 days end (sections 138 and 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act).
You can also file a civil suit to recover the money.

advice.title: If a fundamental right is violated
steps: Write down what happened, when and who was responsible, and keep any documents or other evidence.
Complain to the authority concerned, and where relevant to the National or State Human Rights Commission.
You can file a writ petition in the High Court (Article 226) or directly in the Supreme Court (Article 32) to enforce a fundamental right.
Issues affecting the public at large can be raised as a Public Interest Litigation (PIL).
Free legal help is available from your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA).

advice.title: General guidance: constitutional rights
steps: Fundamental rights are enforced through writ petitions in the High Court or the Supreme Court.
A lawyer or your District Legal Services Authority can tell you whether your case is suitable.
Matters of public importance can be raised as a Public Interest Litigation (PIL).

advice.title: General guidance: going to court
steps: Work out which court has jurisdiction: it depends on where the matter arose, its subject and the amount involved.
Lok Adalats and mediation can settle many disputes faster and without court fees.
Legal Services Authorities give free legal aid to people who are eligible.
